Neural Network Field Guide

Poster

42 architectures and training schemes, from the perceptron (1958) to diffusion LLMs (2025).

Each diagram draws a network in miniature, from input at the bottom to output at the top. In most panels, a circle is one neuron; in sequence models, a column is a token and a circle its whole vector at one layer. A square is larger: an image patch, a matrix-valued state, a whole network (in gray). Color and mark both show a cell’s role, so diagrams read without color. Faded parts play little or no role in the step shown. Parts repeated over positions, windows, copies, or passes share weights; layers, experts, encoders, and decoders drawn alike do not. Sections group by a defining trait: wiring, dynamics, training, cost, or purpose. Years and training methods follow landmark papers, not always the first; many can be trained other ways. Select a diagram for its explanation, key, and papers.

How to read the diagrams

Input

  • Input unit
  • Image patch
  • Noisy input
  • Random noise
  • Visible unit (in and out)
  • Masked token

Hidden

  • Hidden unit
  • Probabilistic hidden
  • Capsule (vector output)
  • Router

State

  • Recurrent unit
  • Memory cell
  • Matrix-valued state

Mixing

  • Attention
  • Convolution or pooling

Output

  • Output unit
  • Reconstruction of input
  • Velocity

Network

  • A whole network

Links

  • Connection
  • Skip connection
  • Data passed on or fed back
  • Gate, acting at the dot
  • Cross-attention, comparison
  • Learnable function
